extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent applicants (including pro se) and patent practitioners preparing U.S. utility patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and requirements for drafting claims and preparing the specification for U.S. utility patent applications, including provisional vs nonprovisional considerations, claim form/structure, antecedent basis, and prosecution strategy. Geared to producing claims that meet 35 U.S.C. §112 and U.S. patent-office practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description and enablement (35 U.S.C. 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification must describe invention and how to make/use it; satisfy both written description and enablement doctrines; disclose best mode (if applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification components and embodiment disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional and nonprovisional components include abstract, drawings (if necessary), and description. Must describe completely a specific embodiment of the process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter or improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the specification contains at least one complete, specific embodiment of the invention (including drawings/examples where necessary) so that claimed subject matter is supported and enabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional: automatically abandoned after one year period; no claims required; written disclosure must meet same requirements as nonprovisional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A provisional filing must still adequately describe and enable the invention; plan for continuity to retain benefit of provisional filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonprovisional application requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonprovisional: at least one claim required; written disclosure must meet requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA) or 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (post-AIA); examined for patentability and can result in a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include at least one claim and ensure the specification satisfies statutory requirements; expect examination for novelty/obviousness and prosecution events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity / priority benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity is key to retaining the benefit of the filing date of the earlier-filed provisional application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on provisional priority, ensure subject matter in the provisional supports all claim elements you expect to claim in the nonprovisional to preserve the earlier filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must define and support claimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is recited in the claims, then it absolutely needs to be described, enabled, and defined by the instant specification. The description should provide clear support for all terms used in the claims so that their meaning may be ascertainable by reference to the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft specification so every claim term has support and explanation; do not claim elements that lack support in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim term interpretation and applicant lexicography
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may serve as their own 'lexicographer.' Claim terms must be given their 'plain meaning,' unless it is inconsistent with the specification. Broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you intend a special definition, define terms explicitly in the specification. Otherwise rely on plain meaning but be aware the office applies the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify invention type and component relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Before drafting claims consider: What is the invention? Tangible: composition, apparatus, machine. Method: making, doing, or using. If tangible, what are the pieces that compose the invention and how do they interrelate? Multiple inventions or multiple versions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this brainstorming to determine claim categories (apparatus, composition, method) and how to structure independent and dependent claims to cover variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim strategy: breadth, variety, and claims budget
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the goals? Obtain the broadest, valid claim(s) possible; obtain claims with a variety of type and scope; not just at filing but during prosecution; consider a claims budget (fees for excess claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan claim scope and types (independent/dependent, method/apparatus/composition) strategically; account for fees (example: micro-entity: independent claims in excess of 3 = $120/claim; each claim in excess of 20 = $25/claim) and prosecution changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear claim construction practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claims early to decide terms; ensure terms are used consistently and captured in the specification; determine which terms need more detailed definition or clarity; description is also provided as drawings and examples; be wary of indefinite language (terms of degree, 'exemplary' language, etc.); ensure that the claims are 'commensurate in scope'; look to U.S. patents as examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent terminology between claims and specification, avoid vague terms of degree, and provide definitions or examples for ambiguous terms to reduce indefiniteness risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim formatting and numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Starts on a separate sheet with the Heading 'Claim Listing'; 1.5 or double spaced; each claim is a single sentence (begins with a capital letter and ends with a period); three independent claims; 20 claims total before excess fees are due; numbered consecutively in ascending order; original numbering preserved throughout prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow formatting rules strictly (single-sentence claims, spacing, heading) and plan claim counts to avoid unexpected excess fees. Preserve original numbering during amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal claim requirements: definiteness and dependency rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonprovisional patent application must have at least one claim which particularly points out and distinctly defines the invention. Claims are written in independent or dependent form. A dependent claim necessarily incorporates by reference all of the limitations of the claim to which it refers. A dependent claim must refer to a preceding claim and must further limit the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure at least one definite independent claim and that dependent claims properly refer to and further limit antecedent claims (do not leave dependent claims indefinite or improperly referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance claim scope (not too specific vs not too general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are too specific may make the invention not valuable; claims that are too general may be not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the broadest claim likely to be allowable, with dependent claims or alternative independent claims to capture narrower fallback positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim structure: preamble guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Every claim contains a preamble (e.g., 'A shovel…' for independent; 'The shovel of claim 1…' for dependent). Carefully consider the language recited in the preamble — effect is determined case-by-case; the preamble is read in the context of the entire claim; recitation may be structural or an intended use/purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft preambles deliberately: choosing e.g., 'A topically-applied composition …' vs 'An ocular composition …' may affect scope and interpretation; consider whether the preamble introduces a structural limitation or only states intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases set forth the scope of the claimed invention. The two most commonly used are 'comprising' (open) and 'consisting of' (closed). 'Comprising' is open-ended and understood as 'including, but not limited to'; 'consisting of' is closed-ended and limits claim elements to those recited. Claims may use both phrases repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose transitional phrase to control whether unrecited elements are excluded ('consisting of') or allowed ('comprising'); use mixed transitions for hybrid scope where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim body requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The body must clearly set forth elements, steps, and/or relationships which are considered to be the claimed invention. Terms/phrases used in the claims must have antecedent basis in the specification. Supported terms/phrases must be described/defined in the specification so their meaning may be ascertained by reference. Limitations should conform to the invention as set forth in the remainder of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List all necessary structural/functional elements and their relationships; ensure each limitation has support and enabling disclosure in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis and internal referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Antecedent basis is referencing within a claim and between claims. Must be first preceded by the indefinite article 'a' or 'an,' or by terminology like 'at least one…,' 'a plurality of…'. Subsequent references should be preceded by the definite article 'the' or 'said' (e.g., 'the at least one…,' 'the plurality of…'). Subsequent references to limitations can occur in both independent and dependent claims. Additional common cue words: 'wherein' or 'whereby.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear antecedent basis for every element to avoid ambiguity (first introduce with 'a' or 'an' or 'at least one,' then refer back with 'the' or 'said').

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative drafting and claim clarity (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iteratively refine claim phrasing and structure to remove grammatical/structural issues (e.g., merge elements, add 'wherein' clauses, avoid stray commas) so the claim reads clearly as a single sentence and the relationships between elements are explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iterative edits to simplify claim sentence structure, make dependencies explicit, and ensure the claim remains a single grammatically-complete sentence that properly limits invention scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting DOs (best practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention. Consider drafting your claims first and then your specification based on terms used in the claims. Review both to make necessary additions and corrections so that the claim terms find support in the specification. Look at the claims in patents issued in your field of technology. Ensure each term has proper antecedent basis. Think about what legal protection you need for your invention and tailor your claims accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these positive practices: draft claims deliberately, ensure spec supports claim language, consult issued patents as models, and tailor claim scope to desired legal protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting cautions / DON'Ts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use claims covering two statutory classes of invention (e.g., 'A widget and method for using same…'). Do not refer back to only a portion of another claim in a dependent claim (e.g., 'The widget of the apparatus of claim 1…'). Do not use terms inconsistently between the claims and/or specification (e.g., visor, visor member, visor section). Do not write multi-sentence claims. Do not 'replace' elements from another claim within a dependent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid these common drafting mistakes to prevent indefiniteness, improper dependency, inconsistent terminology, and invalid claim forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim drafting and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claim examples show that dependent claims must refer to claim 1 (e.g., 'The transdermal patch according to claim 1, wherein...') and add further limitations (e.g., separating layer is between matrix and adhesive layer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting dependent claims, make sure they properly incorporate all limitations of the referenced claim and add further limiting features; use dependent claims to capture fallback positions and particular embodiments.
